summary: BBN's report on ARPANET host status for January 3 to 15, 1972. It was replaced by RFC 298.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 293 records ARPANET host roles and test results from January 3 to January 15, 1972. It updates the host status information in RFC 288 and was later replaced by RFC 298.

questions: what do the arpanet host test codes mean
which rfc replaced the january 1972 host status report
subtitle: A report of ARPANET host status from January 3 to January 15, 1972.

tldr.problem: Network participants needed information about host roles and whether hosts could be reached during the reporting period.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists hosts excluded from daily testing, reported host roles, and daily connection test results for January 3 through January 15.
tldr.outcome: RFC 293 updates RFC 288 and was later obsoleted by RFC 298.

today: RFC 293 updates RFC 288 and was later obsoleted by RFC 298.

sections.title: Hosts Included and Excluded
sections.content:
The report covers the status of most Network Hosts from January 3 to January 15. It excludes hosts not expected to function regularly as servers for at least two weeks, including the BBN PDP-10 (B), Case PDP-10, and the Ames/Paoli systems.

It also excludes Terminal IMPs and hosts intended only as users. The Network Control Center computer is listed as used solely to gather network statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: The report focuses on hosts that could act as servers. It explains that some systems were left out because they were not ready or were intended only as users.

sections.title: Host Roles and Test Codes
sections.content:
A status table lists host roles or predictions, including Server, User Only, and Soon. A separate table gives test results for dates from January 3 through January 15. The codes are O for Open, D for Dead, H for Half Open, R for Refused, and T for Timed out.

Timed out means the destination did not complete the ICP and open a connection within 60 seconds. A marker indicates that a site had announced it might not be available at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables show both reported host roles and actual test results. A timeout means a host did not open a connection within 60 seconds.

sections.title: Updates and Service Notes
sections.content:
The document states that it updates RFC 288. It includes a note that the only service then offered by the UCLA IBM-360/91 was NETRJS, which the BBN Terminal IMP was not equipped to test; the report assumes a successful initial connection to the NETRJS logger indicates that service is functioning.

The host-role table and the daily test table provide different kinds of status information and should be read separately.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 293 updates RFC 288 and explains a limitation in testing the UCLA remote job service. The status table reports host roles, while the test table records connection attempts.

references.text: McKenzie, A., et al., "ARPA Network Handbook", RFC 288, December 1971.
